bibliography.abstract: Pakistan is highly vulnerable to climate change, which points to the need for resilient urban infrastructure and effective stormwater management. This study investigates changes in land use and land cover (LULC) and urban stormwater runoff in Qasimabad, Hyderabad, Pakistan. LULC analysis was conducted with ArcGIS Pro 3.1.5, while hydrological simulation used HEC-HMS 4.11. Changes in LULC were assessed for 2017, 2021, and 2024; hydrological characteristics were examined through flow direction analysis and sub-basin modelling. Across the study period, the spatial distribution of built-up areas, vegetation, water bodies, and bare land changed substantially. Built-up land made up 64.3% of the classified area in 2017. That share was 36.8% in 2021 and 46.2% in 2024, reflecting changes in the mapped land-cover extent alongside continued urban development. Over the same period, population density rose from 8,708 persons per km² in 2017 to 9,963 persons per km² in 2024. Using the HEC-HMS model, seven sub-basins were identified, and peak discharge, runoff timing, and flow characteristics were quantified across the drainage network. When LULC, flow direction, and hydrological modelling were considered together, the analysis showed where runoff was concentrated and where drainage constraints might occur, especially in densely developed areas. These findings can guide urban planners and water resource managers in planning targeted stormwater drainage, protecting natural drainage pathways, and managing flood risk in rapidly developing urban areas.

en.caveats: The land cover analysis shows non-linear shifts in built-up area percentages due to mapping extent differences across the study years, which complicates direct longitudinal comparisons of urban surface expansion.
en.what: The authors mapped land use and land cover shifts and simulated stormwater runoff across seven sub-basins in Qasimabad, Hyderabad, Pakistan, for the years 2017, 2021, and 2024. Using ArcGIS Pro 3.1.5 and HEC-HMS 4.11, the study tracked built-up area fluctuations alongside a population density increase from 8,708 to 9,963 persons per km² to quantify peak discharge and runoff timing across the local drainage network.
en.why: The study spatially isolates specific sub-basins and drainage constraints where rapid population growth and built-environment changes increase stormwater runoff, establishing baseline hydrological metrics for targeted urban flood mitigation in Qasimabad.
